# Film Development Settings: Timings and Due Dates

The **Timings** tab lets OrderHub work out a realistic due date for every film job, based on your lab's real working hours and how long each stage takes. It also records how much hands-on effort each roll needs, so you can see your staffing load.

You'll find it at **Settings** → **Organization** → **Film Development** → **Timings**.



---

## Switching it on

Turn on **Work out film due dates from these timings**. While it's on, film job due dates come from the hours you set here instead of the category lead time. While it's off, due dates work exactly as before.

* Note: Changing these settings doesn't move dates that were already set.

### Your working calendar is used either way

Even with due dates switched off, **Working days**, **Day starts** and **Day finishes** still decide:

* which day's intake batch new film joins, and
* when customer stage messages are sent (see below).

They start at Monday to Friday, 09:00–17:00. Check them even if you don't use due dates.

---

## Setting up your working calendar

1. Under **Working days**, tick the days your lab processes film.
2. Set **Day starts** and **Day finishes** to your production hours.
3. Click **Save timings**.

Only these hours count towards a promise. Evenings, weekends and any days you haven't ticked are skipped. Times use your organisation's time zone.

---

## Hours each stage takes

Each stage has two numbers:

| Column | What it does | Affects due dates? |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Working hours allowed** | How long you allow for the stage, in working hours. The stages are added together to give the customer promise. | Yes |
| **Labour minutes per roll** | Hands-on time one roll takes at that stage. Used for staffing figures only. | Never |

Leave a stage at **0** if it doesn't add time.

* Note: Only stages switched on under **General** → **Stages** are counted. If Receive is off, its hours are ignored. If you turn Develop or Scan off, their hours drop out too.
* Note: When Receive is switched on, its hours count towards every film job's promise, even for an order that goes straight to twin checking without being booked in.

### Print (after scanning)

When print jobs are created automatically from a roll's scans, **Print (after scanning)** sets their due date. The clock starts when that roll's scans arrive, so a delay earlier in the process never makes a print job late on arrival. Print work isn't done in the Film Development App, so it has no labour minutes.

* Note: At **0**, print jobs are promised for the end of the same working day the scans arrive. Set this to your real print turnaround.
* Note: With due dates switched off, these print jobs use the category lead time instead.

---

## How a due date is worked out

1. **The clock starts** when the order is booked in. If you don't book orders in, it starts at the first twin check.
2. **Working hours are added** for each active stage, counting working hours only.
3. **The promise is the end of that working day.** The customer is always promised your **Day finishes** time on the day the hours run out, never a time in the middle of the day.

Film that arrives outside working hours starts the clock at the beginning of the next working day. For example, a Saturday book-in is treated as Monday morning.

### Worked example

Using Monday to Friday, 09:00 to 17:00 (8 working hours a day), with Receive 2, Twin checking 4, Develop 12 and Scan 12 (30 hours in total):

* An order booked in **Monday at 10:00** uses 7 hours on Monday, then 8 on Tuesday, 8 on Wednesday and the last 7 on Thursday. It's promised for **Thursday at 17:00**.
* The same order marked **develop-only** skips Scan's 12 hours, so it's promised for **Wednesday at 17:00**. See *Develop-Only Film (No Scanning)*.

### Set once, never moved

A job's due date is set once, at its first book-in (or first twin check). Booking in a second parcel on the same order doesn't change it, and neither do later twin checks or changes on this tab.

---

## What your team sees in the Film Development App

Timings also drive what operators see at the bench:

* **Due dates in every queue.** Each roll shows its job's due date, and queues are sorted with the earliest due date first. A roll due within the next 24 hours shows **Due** before the date, and a late roll shows **Overdue**.
* **Stage deadlines on each roll.** With due dates switched on, a roll's detail screen has a **Stage deadlines** list. It shows the time by which each stage must be finished to keep the promise, for example "Develop · due Tue 17:00". Finished stages are ticked, and a stage past its deadline is marked **overdue**.



* **The Priority board.** Open **Priority** from the Home screen to see every roll across all stations, grouped by due date. With due dates switched on, a roll that has missed its current stage's deadline shows a **Late at** badge, for example **Late at Develop**. This shows you where the bottleneck is before the final due date is at risk.



* **Metrics.** The **Metrics** screen reports jobs finished on time against their due date, and multiplies your **Labour minutes per roll** by the rolls handled at each stage to show daily hands-on workload.
* **Intake board.** Each day's film is grouped into one batch per working day, using your working calendar. Film booked in on a Saturday joins Monday's batch. If your organisation has more than one lab, each lab has its own daily batch.
* **Customer updates.** If a stage finishes outside your working hours, its customer message waits and is sent when your next working day starts.

* Note: With due dates switched off, the app still shows each job's due date, but there are no stage deadlines or **Late at** badges.

---

## Good to know

* Start with your honest turnaround, not your best case. The promise is only as good as the hours you enter.
* Labour minutes are for planning staff levels. Changing them never changes a customer's due date.
* Changes only affect jobs booked in or twin-checked after you save. Existing due dates stay put.
